marble.name: Simulating chance events
marble.subject: Mathematics
marble.description: Design and use a simulation to estimate the probability of a compound event: choose a random device (coins, dice, spinners, counters drawn with replacement, random-digit tables, or calculator or software random numbers) and a mapping whose probabilities match the situation; define one complete trial (what is generated
marble.prompt: If 40% of blood donors are type A, could you use random numbers or a spinner to act out lots of donor queues, estimate how often at least four donors are needed before the first type A — and explain why doing it again gives a slightly different answer?

authoredAnswer: A suitable fair-bit mapping and three draws per trial; count exactly two heads, divide by complete-trial count. Theoretical 3/8 from three of eight sequences. Different runs vary; larger batches tend to stabilize without guaranteed exactness.

wrongAnswers.revealedBy: Uses elementary draws rather than compound trials as denominator. Source basis: NCETM, KS3 Mastery Professional Development 5.3 Probability (2019), overview pp.2 and sections on theoretical/experimental probability. The
wrongAnswers.fix: Group outputs into complete trials and mark one event result per group; do not reteach coin probability when trial bookkeeping is the issue.

before.name: Probability models
before.reason: Choosing a random device or digit mapping means building a model whose outcome probabilities match the real situation and explaining why it fits

before.name: Percentages as Fractions
before.reason: Turning a percentage such as 40% into a fraction of equally likely digits (4 out of 10) sets up the random-digit mapping

before.name: Tree diagrams
before.reason: Seeing a compound event as a sequence of stages, as in a tree diagram, helps define one complete trial and lets learners compare the estimate with a theoretical value where one exists

before.name: Experimental probability
before.reason: The simulation's estimate is the event's relative frequency over many trials, with more trials giving a more reliable estimate

before.name: How samples vary
before.reason: Explaining why different runs give different estimates draws on the same idea as chance variation between random samples
